unit.title: Formulate a human resource strategic plan

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A ministry's Director of Human Resources is asked to formulate an HR strategic plan. What is its main purpose?
options: To list each officer's leave dates for the year
To set the pay of each officer one by one
To ensure it has the people its goals require
To replace the ministry's strategic business plan

questions.stem: Which document should a government agency's HR strategic plan be built from?
options: Last year's plan for the staff party
The canteen's list of food suppliers
A private company's HR policy manual
The agency's corporate or strategic plan

questions.stem: A parish municipal corporation's corporate plan covers four years. What period should its HR strategic plan usually cover?

Ten years with no review
The same period, reviewed yearly

questions.stem: Before setting HR objectives, an HR manager at a statutory body studies changes in technology, the economy, the law and society that may affect staffing. What is this step called?

options: A promise that nothing will change

questions.stem: Who usually gives final approval to a ministry's HR strategic plan?
options: The newest officer in the HR unit
A supplier of training courses

options: That they match a private firm's policies
That they are as short as possible

options: How many pages the plan had

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What word names the approved list of posts, with their grades, that a public body is allowed to fill?
What two-word term names the step in HR planning that compares the forecast demand for staff with the forecast supply?
In HR planning, what word names the number of staff, and the skills, that an organisation is forecast to need in future?
A department of 160 staff loses 12 staff in a year. What is its turnover rate, as a percentage?
A plan budgets J$6,000,000 to train 400 staff. What is the budget per person, in J$?
What four-letter abbreviation names the computer system used to store and report staff data, such as posts, leave and training?
What word names the forecasting method that uses a fixed relationship, such as one inspector for every 50 premises, to estimate the staff needed?
Of 40 officers who started a training programme, 34 completed it. What is the completion rate, as a percentage?
What two-word term names a group of staff with the potential to fill key posts in future, who are being developed for those posts?

What two-word term names the planned passing of skills and know-how from experienced officers to newer officers before the experienced officers leave?
In a unit of 50 posts, 5 officers retire, 3 resign and 2 are promoted out in one year. What percentage of the unit's posts must be filled?
What word names the HR aim of keeping valued staff from leaving the organisation?

essays.stem: Explain the purpose of an HR strategic plan in a ministry or government agency, and how it should link to the organisation's strategic business plan.
essays.modelAnswer: An HR strategic plan sets out how a ministry or agency will make sure it has the right number of people, with the right skills, in the right places and at the right cost, to achieve its goals over the next three to five years. It moves HR from reacting to vacancies and problems toward planning ahead. It covers how the organisation will attract, develop, deploy, reward and keep its staff, and how it will build a positive working culture. The plan must grow out of the organisation's strategic business plan or corporate plan. For each strategic goal, such as moving services online or extending services to rural parishes, the HR planner asks what people and skills the goal needs, and what changes in numbers, structure or capability follow. The HR objectives are then written to support those goals, and HR actions and budgets are tied to them. The two plans should cover the same period and be reviewed together, so that when the strategy changes, the HR plan changes too. Progress should be reported alongside the corporate plan's measures.
markingPoints: Explains the purpose: right people, skills, places and cost
Notes the move from reactive to planned HR
Shows the plan grows from the strategic or corporate plan
Links HR objectives and actions to strategic goals with an example
Same period, joint review and reporting

essays.stem: Describe the steps you would follow to formulate an HR strategic plan for a government agency, from the first analysis to approval.
essays.modelAnswer: First, I would study the agency's strategic plan and meet senior managers to understand its goals and the people implications. Second, I would carry out an environmental scan, looking at government policy, the economy, technology, labour market trends and the law, and summarise the findings in a SWOT analysis. Third, I would analyse the current workforce: posts and vacancies, ages, skills, turnover, absence and engagement, using the HR information system and a skills audit. Fourth, I would forecast the demand for staff, using ratios, trends and managers' judgement, and the supply, allowing for retirements, resignations and promotions. Fifth, I would compare demand and supply in a gap analysis and set SMART HR objectives to close the most important gaps. Sixth, I would choose strategies for recruitment, retention, development, succession, performance, wellbeing and employee relations, and prepare an implementation plan with actions, owners, timelines, costs, risks and measures. I would consult staff, unions and the central bodies that approve posts and budgets on the draft, revise it, and present it to the Permanent Secretary or head of the agency for approval.
markingPoints: Starts from the strategic plan and senior managers' views
Environmental scan and SWOT
Workforce analysis and demand and supply forecasts
Gap analysis, SMART objectives and strategies
Implementation plan, costing, consultation and approval

essays.stem: An agency forecasts that it will need 330 staff next year. It has 300 now and expects 8% of its current staff to leave during the year. Recruitment costs J$100,000 per new hire, and each new hire needs 5 days of induction training at J$7,000 per day. The budget for recruitment and induction is J$6,000,000. Work out how many staff must be recruited, the total cost, and any shortfall, and recommend what the HR plan should do.
essays.modelAnswer: Expected leavers are 8% of 300, which is 24. The agency must therefore recruit 330 minus 300, which is 30 for growth, plus 24 to replace leavers, giving 54 new hires. Recruitment will cost 54 times J$100,000, which is J$5,400,000. Induction training is 54 times 5 days, which is 270 training days, times J$7,000, which is J$1,890,000. The total cost is J$7,290,000. Against a budget of J$6,000,000, the shortfall is J$1,290,000. The plan should not simply cut induction, because poorly prepared new staff are more likely to leave. Instead, I would recommend several steps. Reducing turnover would cut costs most: if the agency kept 10 more of its staff through better retention, it would need 10 fewer hires and save J$1,350,000. Some posts could be filled by promoting or transferring existing staff, with their posts left vacant if not essential. Recruitment could be phased over two years, filling the most critical posts first, and group induction could lower the cost per day. Finally, the HR director could present the costed case to the budget holders for extra funds.
markingPoints: Correctly finds 24 leavers and 54 new hires
Recruitment cost J$5,400,000 and induction J$1,890,000
Total J$7,290,000 and shortfall J$1,290,000
Recommends sensible options such as retention, internal moves or phasing
Justifies the recommendation and protects essential induction

essays.stem: Explain how an environmental scan and a SWOT analysis feed into the HR objectives of a public hospital's HR strategic plan.
essays.modelAnswer: An environmental scan looks outside the hospital at factors that will affect its workforce over the plan period. These could include government health policy and budgets, the migration of nurses and doctors overseas, the supply of graduates from training schools, new medical technology, changes in employment law and public service rules, and the health needs of an ageing population. Inside, the HR team looks at its own workforce data: vacancies, ages, skills, absence, turnover and staff survey results. A SWOT analysis brings both together. Strengths might be a committed core of experienced nurses and a good training unit; weaknesses might be high vacancy rates in specialist posts and burnout; opportunities might be a partnership with a nursing school; threats might be overseas recruitment of staff. The HR objectives then respond to the most important findings, using strengths and opportunities to deal with weaknesses and threats. For example, an objective might be to cut the vacancy rate for specialist nurses from 20% to 10% within three years through a training partnership and retention measures, and another to reduce sickness absence through a wellbeing programme.
markingPoints: Explains the environmental scan with relevant external factors
Includes internal workforce data
Explains SWOT with hospital examples
Shows how findings lead to priorities
Gives at least one SMART HR objective drawn from the analysis

essays.stem: Compare three methods of forecasting the demand for staff, and recommend which one, or which mix, a tax administration agency should use.
essays.modelAnswer: The ratio method uses a known relationship between workload and staff, such as one case officer for every 80 cases. It is simple and based on data, but it assumes that productivity stays the same, so it can be wrong when new technology or new procedures change how much work each officer can handle. Trend analysis looks at how staff numbers have changed over past years and extends the pattern forward. It is easy to use when data is available, but it assumes the future will be like the past and ignores planned changes, such as a new online filing system. Managerial judgement asks experienced managers to estimate their future needs. It can take account of planned changes and local knowledge, but it may be biased, for example if managers ask for more staff than they need. The Delphi technique improves this by collecting anonymous estimates in rounds until the views agree. For a tax agency, I would recommend a mix: ratios based on forecast caseloads by type of tax, adjusted for expected gains from digital services, then checked through a structured panel of senior managers.
markingPoints: Explains the ratio method with strengths and limits
Explains trend analysis with strengths and limits
Explains managerial judgement or Delphi with strengths and limits
Compares the methods fairly
Recommends a justified mix for the tax agency

essays.stem: A quarter of a government agency's senior officers will reach retirement age within five years. Describe the strategies the HR strategic plan should include to deal with this.
essays.modelAnswer: First, the plan should identify exactly which posts are at risk and when, and rank them by how critical and hard to fill they are. For these key posts, a succession plan should name possible successors and assess how ready they are. A talent pool of promising officers should be developed through a leadership programme, acting appointments, projects, job rotation and coaching, so that several people are ready for each critical post. Knowledge transfer is vital: retiring officers can mentor successors, document key procedures and contacts, and work alongside them for a period before leaving. The agency might also offer some retiring officers part-time or advisory roles, where the rules allow. Where internal candidates are not ready, the plan should prepare for open, merit-based external recruitment early, so that posts are not left empty. Retention of the officers who are developing is also important, through clear career paths and recognition. The plan should cost these actions, set measures such as the share of critical posts with a ready successor, and review progress each year with the senior team.
markingPoints: Identifies and ranks the posts at risk
Succession planning and a developed talent pool
Knowledge transfer from retiring officers
Timely merit-based recruitment and retention of successors
Costs, measures and annual review

essays.stem: Explain why and how stakeholders should be consulted when formulating an HR strategic plan in the public sector.
essays.modelAnswer: Consultation improves the quality of the plan and the chance that it will be carried out. Senior managers know the strategic goals and the people their units will need; line managers and staff know the practical problems; unions and staff associations represent employees' interests and must be engaged on changes to working conditions; and central bodies that approve posts and budgets decide whether proposals can be funded. Other stakeholders may include training institutions and the public who use the services. Without consultation, the plan may rest on wrong assumptions, meet resistance or fail for lack of funds. To consult, the HR director should map the stakeholders and decide how to involve each one. Senior managers could take part in planning workshops, staff could give views through surveys and focus groups, and unions could be briefed and invited to formal meetings. Central bodies should be engaged early, especially on new posts and costs. The draft plan should be shared with clear deadlines for comments. Finally, the HR team should report back on how views were used, revise the plan and keep stakeholders informed during its implementation.
markingPoints: Explains why consultation matters: quality, support and funding
Identifies relevant public sector stakeholders
Uses suitable methods for each group
Engages unions and approving bodies appropriately and early
Reports back and keeps stakeholders informed

essays.stem: Describe the HR measures you would use to monitor a ministry's HR strategic plan, and explain how you would report progress.
essays.modelAnswer: Each HR objective needs at least one measure with a baseline, a target and a date. For staffing, I would use the vacancy rate, the average time to fill posts and the share of critical posts with a ready successor. For retention, I would use the turnover rate overall and for key groups, such as IT officers, together with reasons given in exit interviews. For development, I would track training days per officer, completion rates and whether training closed the skills gaps found in the skills audit. For performance and engagement, I would use the share of officers with agreed work plans and results from a yearly staff survey. For wellbeing, I would measure absence rates and the use of the employee assistance programme. I would also track the cost of the plan against its budget. Data would come from the HR information system, checked for accuracy. I would report quarterly to the senior management team on a one-page dashboard, using red, amber and green to show which measures are on track, with a short explanation and actions for any that are off track, and give a fuller report each year.
markingPoints: Measures have baselines, targets and dates linked to objectives
Includes staffing and retention measures
Includes development, performance or wellbeing measures
Includes cost against budget and reliable data sources
Regular reporting with a dashboard and actions for problems

essays.stem: Set out the main sections of an HR strategic plan document for a government agency, and explain what each section should contain.
essays.modelAnswer: The plan would open with a foreword from the head of the agency and an executive summary giving the main objectives, actions and costs. The introduction would explain the purpose of the plan, the period it covers and how it links to the agency's strategic plan. The context section would summarise the environmental scan and SWOT analysis. The workforce profile would describe the current staff: numbers against the establishment, vacancies, ages, skills, turnover, absence and survey results. The workforce forecast and gap analysis section would set out the forecast demand and supply of staff and the main gaps. The HR objectives section would list SMART objectives linked to strategic goals. The strategies section would explain how each objective will be met, covering recruitment, retention, learning and development, succession, performance, wellbeing, employee relations and HR systems. The implementation plan would give actions, owners, timelines and resources, often with a Gantt chart. The budget section would cost the plan. The risk section would list the main risks and responses. Finally, the monitoring and review section would give measures, targets and reporting dates.
markingPoints: Summary, introduction and link to the strategic plan
Context, workforce profile, forecast and gap analysis
SMART objectives and strategies
Implementation plan, budget and risks
Monitoring and review arrangements

essays.stem: Evaluate the main risks to carrying out an HR strategic plan in a public body, and recommend how to manage them.
essays.modelAnswer: One major risk is a lack of funds: budgets may be cut or posts not approved, leaving the plan unaffordable. This is managed by costing every action, ranking actions by their impact on strategic goals, engaging the approving bodies early and having a phased fallback plan. A second risk is that forecasts prove wrong, for example if more staff leave than expected because of overseas recruitment. Regular monitoring of turnover and exit reasons, and scenarios for higher losses, reduce this risk. A third risk is weak support from senior managers, who may see HR planning as an HR task only; giving each director ownership of relevant actions and reporting progress to the senior team helps. A fourth risk is resistance from staff or unions to changes such as new roles; early consultation and clear communication reduce it. A fifth risk is poor HR data, which leads to bad decisions; data quality checks and an improved HR information system are the remedy. Finally, changes in government policy, such as a merger, may make the plan out of date, so the plan should be reviewed at least yearly. A risk register should record owners and actions.
markingPoints: Funding risk with a suitable response
Forecast or turnover risk with a suitable response
Leadership support or resistance risk with a suitable response
Data or policy change risk with a suitable response
Uses a risk register with owners and regular review

practical1.title: Carry out a workforce and gap analysis for a government agency's HR plan
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case pack for a made-up government agency (for example a parish municipal corporation, a regional health authority or a licensing agency), with its strategic goals for the next three years, an establishment list, staff data in a spreadsheet (posts, staff in post, ages, grades, leavers and absence for three years), workload figures and a summary of a staff survey. As a group, produce: a workforce profile sheet showing the vacancy rate, turnover, absence rate and the share of staff aged 55 or over, each worked out and checked twice; a SWOT poster for the agency's workforce; a demand forecast for two key job groups using a workload ratio, with your assumptions written down; a supply forecast allowing for retirements and turnover; a gap analysis table; and five SMART HR objectives linked to the strategic goals. Give each member a named role: data analyst (workforce profile), environment lead (SWOT poster), forecaster (demand and supply), gap analyst (gap table), and objectives writer. In a group of four, the gap analyst also writes the objectives. Each member explains their part to the assessor.
materials: Case pack and staff data spreadsheet from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software
Poster paper, markers and sticky notes
photos: The workforce profile sheet on screen with the rates worked out
The demand forecast with its written assumptions
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Vacancy, turnover, absence and age figures are correct
The SWOT analysis reflects the case and separates internal from external factors
Demand and supply forecasts are worked out correctly and assumptions are stated
The gap analysis follows from the forecasts
The objectives are SMART and linked to the strategic goals
Explained their part clearly when the assessor asked
safety: Use only the made-up staff data; no real officers' records
Treat the staff data as confidential and keep it on Centre computers
Discuss the case respectfully and value every member's view
Share the workload fairly and take short screen breaks

practical2.title: Draft an HR strategic plan summary and present it to a senior management panel (role play)
practical2.brief: Using the assessor's case pack for a made-up public body (or your Practical 1 findings, if the assessor agrees), your group drafts the core of an HR strategic plan and presents it to a senior management panel, played by the assessor as the Permanent Secretary or head of the body. First, hold a 15-minute consultation meeting with a staff association representative (played by a member of another group) on two proposals in your plan, and record the views raised and how you will respond. Then produce: a strategies table showing, for each of four HR objectives, the strategies and actions chosen; a three-year Gantt chart of the actions; a costing spreadsheet for the first year, with every sum worked out and checked twice and compared with the budget in the case pack; a risk register with at least five risks, owners and responses; a one-page set of measures with baselines, targets and reporting dates; and a ten-minute presentation. Give each member a named role: plan lead (chairs the consultation and leads the presentation), strategies writer, finance officer (costing), risk officer (risk register), and monitoring officer (measures and Gantt chart). In a group of four, the plan lead also does the Gantt chart. Every member presents their part and answers at least one question from the panel.
materials: Case pack with budget figures from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet, word-processing and presentation software
Note sheets for the consultation meeting
Gantt chart and risk register templates (optional)
photos: The consultation meeting, with the notes of views raised and responses
The costing spreadsheet compared with the budget
The presentation to the panel, with the slides showing
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Strategies clearly address each objective and fit public service rules
The consultation was respectful and views were recorded and answered
The costing is complete, correct and compared with the budget
Risks are realistic and have owners and responses
Measures have baselines, targets and reporting dates
Presented their part clearly and answered the panel's questions
safety: Use only the made-up case and invented names
Keep consultation notes and plan figures confidential to the group and assessor
Keep the role play respectful; disagree with proposals, not with people
Plan the work so that no member is overloaded, and take breaks
